questions.prompt: You run claude in default mode and ask for poem.txt. Before the file exists, Claude shows a prompt. What does that prompt mean?
questions.explain: The harness stops between the model's tool request and the write, and waits for your answer. Until you answer yes, nothing is written.

options.text: The harness is waiting for your answer before the write happens
The file is already written and the prompt asks whether to keep it
options.misconception: The write is held back until you approve it.

options.text: The model is unsure what to write and needs a better prompt
options.misconception: The prompt comes from the harness and concerns permission, not the model's confidence.

options.text: The operating system is blocking the write
options.misconception: That would be a sandbox refusal. This prompt comes from the harness.

questions.prompt: You ask for a poem file in plan mode, decline the plan, and run ls. What do you expect?
questions.explain: Plan mode lets Claude read and propose. Edits wait for an approved plan, so declining leaves the folder unchanged.

options.text: No poem file, because nothing is edited until a plan is approved
An empty poem file, created so the plan has a target
options.misconception: Plan mode creates nothing before you approve.

options.text: The finished poem file, written while the plan was shown
options.misconception: A plan is a proposal, so no write happens during it.

questions.prompt: Sort each guard by what enforces it.
questions.explain: Permission modes and rules belong to the harness and govern its tools. The sandbox is enforced by the operating system around shell commands.

items.misconception: A permission rule is a harness setting.

items.text: The prompt before a file is written in default mode
items.misconception: The prompt is the harness checking its permission rules.

items.text: touch ~/sandbox-probe failing with Operation not permitted
items.misconception: A sandbox boundary is enforced by the operating system, whatever the model asked for.

items.text: curl failing with Could not resolve host in the sandbox
items.misconception: The sandbox cuts network access at the operating-system level.

questions.prompt: A deny rule blocks Read(./.env). An approved Python one-liner opens .env itself, outside a sandbox. What happens?
questions.explain: A Read rule limits Claude's file tools and the file commands it recognises, such as cat. It cannot see inside a program that opens the file itself. The sandbox limits writes and network access, and by default it still lets programs read most files.

options.text: The program can still read it, because the rule cannot see inside a program
The program fails, because a deny rule covers every way of reading that file
options.misconception: Rules cover the file tools and recognised file commands, not what an arbitrary program opens.

options.text: Claude asks again, because deny rules only apply to the first read
options.misconception: A deny rule is checked on every matching request. It does not apply to other tools.

questions.prompt: You are on native Windows and run /sandbox, then ask Claude to run touch on a file in your home folder. What should you expect?
questions.explain: On native Windows Claude Code runs commands without a sandbox. Use WSL 2 to get one.

options.text: The command runs unsandboxed, so use WSL 2 for the sandbox
The command is refused, as it would be on macOS
options.misconception: The sandbox is not available on native Windows.

options.text: Windows has its own built-in sandbox that Claude Code switches on
options.misconception: Claude Code does not use one on native Windows.

questions.prompt: A colleague says they run claude with --dangerously-skip-permissions in a container, so it is safe. What still applies?
questions.explain: The container limits the machine, and the agent can still change the mounted project folder. Anything inside the container, including credentials, can be reached by a malicious project.

options.text: It can still change the mounted folder and reach what is in the container
Nothing, because a container makes every file and prompt harmless
options.misconception: A container is a boundary, and what is inside it stays exposed.

options.text: The flag stops working in a container, so permission prompts return
options.misconception: The flag is intended for containers and works there.

questions.prompt: In OpenCode you set a `read` deny rule for `*.env`. The agent then runs `cat .env` as a shell command. What happens?
questions.explain: A rule blocks the action it names. `read` covers the read tool, and `cat` runs under the `shell` action, so it needs its own rule. Even then, a program that opens the file itself gets through.

options.text: The file prints, because the rule covers the read tool and not shell commands
The command is blocked, because a read rule covers every way of reading the file
options.misconception: The read action covers the read tool. A shell command is a different action.

options.text: OpenCode asks you first, because denied paths always prompt before anything runs
options.misconception: A deny rule refuses. It does not prompt. Here no rule matches the shell command, and the default policy allows it.

questions.prompt: You set an `edit` rule to `ask`, then run `opencode run` with a prompt that writes a file. What do you see?
questions.explain: A non-interactive run cannot ask, so OpenCode rejects the request. Start the interactive interface to see the prompt itself.

options.text: The request is rejected and no file is written, because the run cannot ask you
The file is written anyway, because the default policy allows every edit without asking
options.misconception: Your rule overrides the default for edits, and the rule says ask.

options.text: A prompt appears in the terminal and the run waits there for your answer
options.misconception: opencode run is non-interactive. The prompt appears only in the interactive interface.

questions.prompt: Match each permission mode to what it does.
questions.explain: Modes trade convenience for control. Plan mode is the safest for first contact.

pairs.right: Asks before edits, shell commands and network requests
Auto-accepts file edits and common file commands
pairs.misconception: acceptEdits accepts edits without prompting. plan is the read-only mode.

pairs.right: Reads and proposes; no edits until you approve a plan
Skips most prompts; for containers and virtual machines only
pairs.misconception: bypassPermissions removes the safety prompts, which is why it belongs in disposable environments.
